question: What does the resurrection evidence actually support?
aliases: did Jesus rise from the dead
do I have to believe in the resurrection
finding: Something happened after the crucifixion that convinced a shattered group of Jewish followers their teacher was alive and vindicated. We take that seriously, and we don't claim to know what it was. The sources describe appearances, not an examined body, and they describe them inconsistently and with increasing detail the later they were written. Our claim is narrower: salvation in Jesus's own recorded teaching never depends on believing a historical event. Asked how to obtain eternal life he answered "keep the commandments." In the forty days the texts give him after the resurrection, he commissions repentance, forgiveness, service and the kingdom, and never once tells anyone to believe his death was a payment for sin. The requirement to affirm the event as the condition of salvation is Pauline and then Nicene. It is not his.
oneLiners: We're not saying it didn't happen. We're saying nothing in his own words makes your standing with God depend on your opinion about it.
If believing in the resurrection were the saving message, forty days was the time to say it. He talked about the kingdom.
The first gospel ends by telling you to go to Galilee and see him, and then stops without showing you. The appearances get described, and get physical, as the decades pass.

The creed in 1 Corinthians 15 is probably from within five years of the crucifixion, and we'll say that for you. It uses the same word for Peter's experience and Paul's, and Paul's was a light and a voice.
The risen Jesus handed the power to forgive sins to his friends. No blood in that sentence.
doNotSay: Don't say Mark knows no appearance tradition. Mark 14:28 and 16:7 point to Galilee. The claim is about what Mark narrates, not what he knows.
Don't hide the early date of the 1 Corinthians 15 creed. State it yourself; it proves the speed of the conviction, not the nature of the event.
Don't dodge Luke 24:26 and 24:46-47. Concede that Luke reads the suffering as necessary; then read what gets proclaimed: repentance.
Don't use the podcast-archive Tabor episodes as sources. Background only; auto-captioned.

sources.phrase: observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you
sources.note: The commission is the commandments. If believing in the atoning death were the saving message, this was the moment and this was the audience.

sources.tier: red text · after the resurrection · John
sources.note: Forgiveness delegated directly to human beings with no blood mechanism attached. (Demoted under the how-we-read-John rule; Matthew 18:18 and 6:14-15 carry the point without it.)

sources.phrase: pertaining to the kingdom of God
sources.note: Forty days, "speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God."

sources.tier: red text · after the resurrection · own it
sources.note: Concede the obvious half: Luke's risen Jesus reads the suffering as scripturally necessary (24:26, 24:46). Then read the rest: what gets proclaimed is repentance. Not belief in a transaction. "Necessary that he suffer" and "believe his death paid your debt" are two different claims.
He answered the salvation question before the cross existed as a doctrine. A condition anyone in any century can meet; no historical event has to be verified first.

Mark ends here in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus: a forward reference to Galilee (16:7) and no narrated encounter. Then watch the development: Matthew's mountain where "some doubted" (28:17); Luke and John's touching, wound inspection, broiled fish. The appearances get more corporeal, more detailed and less geographically consistent as the sources get later.

sources.phrase: tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem
sources.note: Mark and Matthew send the disciples to Galilee; Luke tells them to stay in Jerusalem (also Acts 1:4). One of those gospels is wrong about where the most important event in history happened.

sources.title: Gospel of Thomas 70 and 1
sources.note: 114 sayings, no passion narrative, no empty tomb, no appearances, no atonement. Whatever its date, an early Jesus community built its entire soteriology without the event. Don't argue Thomas's priority here.

"If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile." Paul's criterion, inside Paul's system, the same one that makes confession the mechanism (Romans 10:9). Jesus, asked the identical question, pointed to the commandments. Prefer Paul's standard if you like, but say so, because only one of them comes from Jesus.

sources.phrase: Ought not Christ to have suffered
sources.note: "Your own gospel says the cross was required." Granted. "Necessary" in Luke is scriptural fulfillment, not penal substitution, which needs a further claim Luke never makes. Three verses later what is proclaimed is repentance (24:47).

sources.tier: what Paul taught · the five hundred
sources.note: "The minimal-facts case: empty tomb, appearances, five hundred witnesses." Appearance claims are good evidence of experiences people couldn't explain. They cannot discriminate between a body and a vision, because the sources use one verb for both. The five hundred are never named, located or interviewed; they appear once, in a list, in a letter.

sources.tier: KJV prints it · absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus
sources.note: The longer ending, 16:9-20. The KJV has it; our two oldest complete Greek codices don't; nearly every modern Bible brackets it (Ehrman and the committees of believing scholars agree). "The disciples died for this": sincerity establishes belief, not accuracy, which is what we concede. The tomb narratives strain: three women and a young man; an earthquake and an angel; two men; Mary alone, then two angels.

sources.title: Didache 1-6 and 9-10: no creed, no resurrection requirement
sources.note: "Denying the bodily resurrection means you aren't a Christian." We're not denying it; we decline to make an unverifiable event the gate, because the earliest Christians didn't. The pre-baptismal catechism has no creed and no resurrection requirement. The "unless you affirm X" line enters with Paul and hardens at Nicaea.

sources.tier: what Paul taught · the creed, mid-30s
sources.note: Received tradition (παρέλαβον / παρέδωκα), Aramaic "Cephas", dated by Lüdemann, Hengel and Habermas alike to within two to five years of the crucifixion. Granted loudly. One verb, ōphthē, for Cephas, the Twelve, the five hundred and Paul himself. Pushing it back to the 30s makes the problem older, not smaller: the earliest formula reports appearances in language that cannot distinguish a body from a vision. ("Died for our sins" is inside the formula too; early attestation of an interpretation is not Jesus teaching it.)

Paul's own experience is a light and a voice, and Acts has him call it exactly that: "the heavenly vision." He places it in the same grammatical category as everyone else's (Tabor, Paul and Jesus, 2012).
